svg.text: Routes: speed, first pass, and the angle of the needle
Onset, fastest to slowest
INTRAVENOUS — seconds. No absorption step at all; the dose is already in the blood.
INHALED / SUBLINGUAL — minutes. Rich blood supply, and both bypass the liver.
INTRAMUSCULAR — 10 to 20 minutes. Muscle is well perfused.
SUBCUTANEOUS — slower and steadier. Fat is poorly perfused, which is the point for insulin.
ORAL — slowest and least predictable, because food, gut motility and the liver all interfere.
First pass metabolism
A drug swallowed goes gut, then portal vein,
then LIVER, and only then the body.
The liver destroys part of the dose before it
ever acts — which is why the oral dose of a
drug is often far larger than its IV dose.
Routes that escape the liver first
Sublingual and buccal — straight into veins
under the tongue
Rectal — partly
Intravenous, intramuscular, subcutaneous,
transdermal, inhaled
The needle angle
INTRADERMAL 10-15 degrees
SUBCUTANEOUS 45 degrees
INTRAMUSCULAR 90 degrees
Intradermal raises a visible bleb — if no bleb appears, you went too deep and the test is invalid.
Intramuscular sites, and the one that is safest
VENTROGLUTEAL is preferred for adults: no large nerves or vessels, and it takes the largest volume.
VASTUS LATERALIS, the outer thigh, is the site for infants. DELTOID takes small volumes only, up to 1 mL.
Dorsogluteal, the old upper-outer buttock, is avoided — the sciatic nerve is too close.
